query: Research on refractory multicomponent alloys has emphasized exceptional strength at room and elevated temperatures, while mechanical assessment has relied mainly on compression and has included relatively few tensile studies. WFeNiMo fragments released more chemical energy than tungsten-alloy fragments in thin-steel-target penetration tests, and HfZrTiTa0.53 was reported at 786 MPa yield strength, 1314 MPa compressive strength, and 13.5% terminal strain. This evidence establishes strength and energetic promise but leaves limited tensile ductility, load-bearing reliability, and processability unresolved. Subject to preserving strength and impact-triggered energy release, what single testable hypothesis identifies an intervention for HfZrTiTa0.53 that could improve tensile ductility and uniform elongation? Include the intervention, causal mechanism, directional or quantitative outcomes relative to the reported baseline, the applicable temperature, loading mode, and strain-rate limits, prior evidence from the cited studies, and matched compression, tension, and impact tests with a result that would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: Applying a deep cryogenic treatment (DCT) to HfZrTiTa0.53 alloy samples will improve their tensile ductility and uniform elongation without significantly degrading their high yield strength or impact-triggered energy release.
generation.material_initial_state: HfZrTiTa0.53 alloy produced by conventional processing (similar in baseline performance to reported values: 786 MPa yield strength, 1314 MPa compressive strength, and 13.5% terminal strain measured under compression)
generation.intervention: Expose the alloy samples to deep cryogenic treatment (e.g., immersion in liquid nitrogen for a duration on the order of 24 hours) as a single modification step.
generation.conditions: Room temperature tensile testing under quasi‐static strain rates; additional matched compression and impact tests should be performed to verify that the energy release capability is preserved and that the treatment does not impair load-bearing reliability.
generation.structural_mediator: Enhanced lattice distortion and induced microstructural changes (such as refined dislocation structures or twin boundaries) that facilitate additional slip systems.
generation.mechanism: DCT is proposed to relieve residual stresses and induce a beneficial phase transition or refinement in the microstructure. This process is expected to increase the number of available slip systems and delay the onset of localized failure, thereby improving tensile ductility and uniform elongation while maintaining strength and impact-triggered energy release.
generation.predicted_outcome: Under room temperature tensile testing, DCT-treated HfZrTiTa0.53 should exhibit a measurable increase in uniform elongation (for example, an improvement in elongation by approximately 10–20% relative to the untreated baseline) with only minimal changes (within ±5%) to yield strength and retained high impact energy release characteristics.
generation.baseline: Untreated HfZrTiTa0.53 alloy showing a yield strength of 786 MPa, compressive strength of 1314 MPa, and 13.5% terminal strain.
generation.boundary: This improvement is expected only under room temperature and quasi-static tensile loading; effects at elevated temperatures or under high strain-rate conditions are not addressed by this hypothesis.
generation.uncertainty: The precise quantitative improvement in tensile ductility and the stability of the induced microstructural changes under varying processing conditions remain uncertain, and the impact on long‐term load-bearing reliability requires further validation.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of HfZrTiTa0.53 alloy samples using the same processing method. Apply the deep cryogenic treatment (e.g., 24-hour soak in liquid nitrogen) to one set, while keeping the other set untreated. Perform matched tests including room temperature quasi‐static tensile tests, compression tests, and impact energy release tests. Conduct microstructural analysis (e.g., electron microscopy) to compare dislocation structures and phase characteristics.
measurements: Tensile elongation (uniform elongation and total strain at failure)
Impact energy release using a standardized drop hammer or similar apparatus
Microstructural characterization (e.g., via SEM or TEM)
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the DCT-treated samples do not exhibit at least a ~10% increase in uniform tensile elongation relative to untreated samples, or if there is a reduction in yield strength or impact energy release beyond ±5% of the untreated baseline, the hypothesis would be falsified.

## Abstract
AbstractHfNbTaTiZr high-entropy alloy has wide application prospects as a biomedical material, and the use of laser additive manufacturing can solve the forming problems faced by the alloy. In view of the characteristics of the one-time forming of additive manufacturing methods, it is necessary to develop non-mechanical processing modification methods. In this paper, deep cryogenic treatment (DCT) is first applied to the modification of a HEA with BCC structure, then the post-processing method of DCT is combined with laser melting deposition (LMD) technology to successfully realize the coordinated improvement of forming and strength–ductility synergistic improvement in lightweight Hf0.25NbTa0.25TiZr alloy. The final tensile strength of the alloy after DCT treatment is 25% higher than that of the as-cast alloy and 11% higher than that of the as-deposited alloy, and the elongation is increased by 48% and 10%, respectively. In addition, DCT also achieves induced phase transition without additional deformation.Keywords: laser melting deposition, high entropy alloy, deep cryogenic treatment, 3D printing, defects, strength–ductility synergistic improvement
## 1. Introduction

HfNbTaTiZr high-entropy alloy can be improved by increasing the lattice distortion of the alloy []. The above characteristics mean more modification methods can be applied to Hf-Nb-Ta-Ti-Zr alloys.
At present, the casting forming of HEAs is facing some problems due to their high melt viscosity, and laser additive manufacturing (AM) technology can effectively solve this problem [,,]. Laser melting deposition (LMD) technology has high energy density and complex-shape-forming ability, which can solve the problem of HEA forming and accumulate thermal stress in as-deposited alloy samples [].
